newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia likely to impose forex controls -analysts.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia likely to impose forex controls -analysts.

text.p: Malaysia is likely to introduce measures to ward off a fresh speculative attack on the ringgit despite the recent strengthening of the currency, analysts said at the weekend.
Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad had earlier in the week hinted of possible punitive action against currency speculators but did not offer specifics.
Analysts said it would be foolish to rule out the possibility of anti-speculation measures being introduced.

"The fact that this (warning) was coming from the prime minister, you have to take it seriously. There's a strong possibility of new measures being introduced," said Derrick Lee, senior analyst at market analysis firm Technical Data.
Players are still guessing what kind of foreign exchange controls Malaysia is likely to introduce.

Speculation has been rife that Malaysia may soon impose a restriction similar to the one imposed in Singapore on foreign-exchange swaps, which are forward agreements on exchanging one currency to another.

An onshore bank in Singapore is only allowed to quote to offshore parties the sale side of the swap deal for a maximum $5 million per day, thus preventing internationalisation of the local currency and dampening speculative moves.
Mahathir said last week that Malaysians had some complicity in the attack on the ringgit by making the local currency available to the speculators.
"A swap restriction would be an appropriate solution to that," said Sani Hamid, an analyst at research house MMS International.
Southeast Asian currencies came under speculative attack early this summer, resulting in de facto devaluations of the Thai baht and the Philippine peso.
Indonesia widened the trading band for the rupiah and the "safe-haven" Singapore dollar also fell sharply.
The ringgit fell more than five percent during the period to a three-year low of 2.6530 to a dollar. It closed at 2.6290/320 in Kuala Lumpur on Friday.
Bank Negara Malaysia, the central bank, has spent $2-3 billion defending the ringgit in the past few weeks.
Analysts said the imposition of foreign exchange restrictions was not unprecedented in Malaysia.

In February 1989, Bank Negara imposed a daily limit on non-trade-related swaps -- on the sale side -- that commercial banks could undertake with offshore banks of up to $2 million per offshore customer.
The limits were extended to cover the bid side in June 1992.

And faced with a strong flow of short-term money into the country in 1994, Bank Negara imposed negative interest rates on foreign deposits, banned swaps trading and stopped foreigners from buying Malaysian government paper.
Analysts said this time around there was also talk that Malaysia would introduce capital tax on "vostro" accounts, which are ringgit accounts held by foreigners.
But analysts said foreign investment, which has been one of the driving forces behind the country's buoyant economy, will be severely jolted by any foreign exchange controls.

"They will have to consider very carefully any measures at this point of time...unless they are willing to take a step back in growth," said Philip Wee, regional treasury economist at Standard Chartered Bank in Singapore.
-- Kuala Lumpur newsroom (603-201 4813)
